authoring.question: q-84607
authoring.value:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & ∗ \\ 0 & 1 & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the third column of the matrix $P.$
authoring.rationale: The original P columns (1,1,0) and (1,0,0) have eigenvalues 5 and 3, contrary to D=diag(3,5,-1), so no third column can satisfy the literal request. The explicitly authorized minimum correction swaps only those two fixed P columns. The third column (-2,1,2) is unchanged and satisfies Av=-v; MA actually graded option b Correct, and its revealed worked solution independently yields that vector. Its narrative mistakenly says A-(-4)I even though its displayed calculation uses A-(-1)I, and its final P mistakenly has -1 in the first row of the second column; both are corrected to match the eigenvalue calculation. All raw MA captures, grades, history, uncertain solver files and accepted answer remain unchanged. All field and answer identities remain unchanged because their values/key do not change.

decisions.reason: Retain the verified mathematical correction instead of reimporting the source error

authoring.value:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=5,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ 

So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{3}I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations whose augmented matrix $M$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix is already  in row echelon form.  It has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.  From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{4}(-2(\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3})-3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(-4{x}_{3}) \\  & =-{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$
